steps.action:
# The Last Rotation

Every morning, Maren climbed the 112 steps to extinguish the light.

Every evening, she climbed them again to wake it.

This had been her life for eleven years on Sorrow Point, a finger of rock that jutted into the North Atlantic like something the continent had tried to shake off. The Coast Guard had offered her a transfer twice. She had declined twice. They had stopped asking.

People assumed she was lonely. She let them assume.

What they didn't understand was the weight of responsibility — how it anchored you better than any company could. Ships moved through that darkness trusting her. Fishermen with children at home trusted her. She was the fixed point around which dangerous things safely turned, and there was a dignity in that so profound she sometimes felt it in her sternum like a second heartbeat.

On a Tuesday in November, she spotted a dinghy through the fog. One man. Bailing with a coffee can.

She put the rescue boat in the water herself.

He was a lobsterman named Claude, half-frozen and embarrassed. She gave him dry clothes, soup, and silence — which he seemed to need as much as the warmth.

Before the helicopter came for him, he looked up at the tower.

"God," he said quietly. "I've never been so glad to see anything in my life."

Maren nodded.

That was the whole explanation. That was all of it.
